  You are revising ADR-0016 at D:/the-synaptic-sea-2d/docs/architecture/adr-0016-restore-ordering-and-cross-block-verification.md (project D:/the-synaptic-sea-2d, Godot 4.7.2 GDScript) after per-ADR engine and TD-ADR reviews and a cross-ADR adjudication of the Core tier. Autonomous mode: "Revise flagged items". Apply every BLOCKING finding and every ruling you own; align your references to rulings owned by other ADRs without taking over their decisions; apply non-blocking findings unless clearly wrong (decline with a reason).   ADR-0016 review verdict CONCERNS (engine): no blocking engine error. No API is deprecated, post-cutoff or mis-signed. The probed claims P1 and P3 reproduce on 4.7.2. Seven non-blocking amendments are needed before Acceptance. Three matter most: packed-array reference semantics at restore (E3), the blind spot in the KRN-RST-10 leak guard (E4), and one non-compiling Key Interfaces listing (E1).:
  E1 [low] Key Interfaces puts `class_name LoadStage` and `class_name LoadFailure` under a single `# src/kernel/load_stage.gd` header. A GDScript file allows one `class_name`, so copying the block verbatim will not parse. The other listings (RestorePlan, BlockIdOrder, VerifyOut, FixtureFactory) each have a header and are fine. The `LoadStage` int constants are legal GDScript.
    amendment: Add a `# src/kernel/load_failure.gd` header above `class_name LoadFailure`. State that each listed class is its own file, as ADR-0003 does for fault classes.
  E2 [medium] The Key Interfaces use bare `Array` and `Dictionary`: `RestorePlan.compile(blocks: Array, max_blocks: int, out_errors: Array)`, `LoadFailure.detail: Dictionary`, and `restore(data: Dictionary, ...)`. All of these sit in `src/kernel` or `src/shared`. ADR-0010 SIM-09 bans bare `Array` and undeclared bare `Dictionary` there, so the ADR's own interface listing fails the lint. If `blocks` becomes `Array[BlockDescriptor]`, every caller must pass a typed array. A bare literal is rejected for a typed-array parameter.
    amendment: Type the parameters: `blocks: Array[BlockDescriptor]` and `out_errors: Array[String]`, or a typed `BootError` record. Add `LoadFailure.detail` and the `restore` payload to the `dictionary_variant.json` allow-list, or reduce `detail` to a small typed record (reason, a, b). Tell the stories that callers build typed arrays.
  E3 [medium] Packed arrays AND Array/Dictionary are reference types in GDScript. Probed on 4.7.2: after `block.col = payload["col"]`, a write to `block.col[0]` changed `payload["col"]`. An alias taken from a member also writes through to it, and a nested `Array` stored via `b.d = payload` aliases the payload. Section 3.1 phase 2 says `restore` "copies the contents into the existing block object" but does not require a deep copy. If a block assigns the staged columns by reference, then: (a) the live block aliases the payload that Save/Load or the single re-armed `SnapshotContext` put-slot still holds; (b) a default payload shared with a static or const default becomes mutable global state; (c) FixtureFactory `typical()` and `extreme()` results get mutated by the round trip, which can hide or fake idempotence failures. The same applies to `binding_source`: `ctx.put(PackedInt64Array)` hands the kernel a reference. If an owner returned a member array, the kernel would read live state, so it must be a fresh array per call (the ADR says 'derived per call'; make it a rule).
    amendment: Add to section 3.1 and the Implementation Guidelines: 'phase 2 copies by value. Packed columns are assigned from `.duplicate()` or rebuilt element by element, and nested Array/Dictionary are deep-copied. A block must never retain a reference to `data` or any of its members.' The kernel clears the `ctx.put` slot immediately after applying a `default_state` payload and before it re-arms the same context for `restore`. FixtureFactory methods return a fresh payload on every call. `binding_source` builds a new `PackedInt64Array` per call. Add one KRN-RST test: mutate the block after restore and assert that the payload bytes are unchanged.
  E4 [medium] KRN-RST-10's leak guard (`OBJECT_COUNT`, `OBJECT_NODE_COUNT`, `OBJECT_ORPHAN_NODE_COUNT`) only sees Object-derived leaks. P3 reproduces: 100 two-object RefCounted cycles gave a delta of 200 (the monitor returns float, `200.0`). Two other cycle types are not caught. 1,000 self-referencing Dictionary and Array pairs left OBJECT_COUNT at 0 and raised static memory by 612,192 bytes. A RefCounted that stores a lambda capturing `self` leaks one object per instance (delta 100 for 100 instances), so lambdas capturing `self` need a ban. Section 3.1's rule 'no reference cycle in scratch' and Verification 5 therefore claim more than the test can check. ADR-0010 already records this limit (P6, CNT-02).
    amendment: Extend KRN-RST-10 with the ADR-0010 CNT-02 `MEMORY_STATIC` tolerance check (debug and editor binaries only; release availability is UNVERIFIED there). Compare with `int()` casts, because `get_monitor` returns float. Add a lint or review rule: no self-referencing container in restore scratch, and no lambda or `Callable` capturing `self` stored in a RefCounted member. State that `OBJECT_COUNT` detects Object cycles only.
  E5 [low] P4 is true but vacuous. Headless, `RENDER_TEXTURE_MEM_USED` reads `0.0` because the renderer is the dummy one (reproduced). A baseline `OBJECT_ORPHAN_NODE_COUNT` of 1 appeared even in a bare `--script` run, so cycle-1 versus cycle-n comparison must use deltas. 'Readable headless' does not mean 'measurable headless'. The node-count and render-texture legs that ADR-0028 adds cannot be validated in lane H. Whether `OBJECT_ORPHAN_NODE_COUNT` is populated in release exports is UNVERIFIED.
    amendment: Reword P4 to: 'the monitors return values headless but render monitors are 0 under the dummy renderer; render-texture legs run in the windowed lane W (ADR-0010 § 8)'. Specify KRN-RST-10 as a delta against cycle 1, not an absolute number. Mark the orphan monitor as debug-binary only.
  E6 [medium] R1 check (a), 'every payload key names a registered block', does not say what order the payload keys are visited in. Dictionary iteration is insertion order, which is decoder order, so which unknown block gets named depends on the file's key order. Section 5.5 and KRN-RST-12 claim the first failure is a pure function of the payload, and section 2.2 says 'Dictionary iteration never decides anything'. Payload keys may also arrive as `String` where the registry holds `StringName`. ADR-0005 line 775 notes a Dictionary treats equal text as the same key, so lookup works, but ordering does not.
    amendment: Specify R1 as follows. Check (a) iterates the payload's keys converted to `String` and sorted by `BlockIdOrder`. Checks (b) to (d) iterate the registry in `RestorePlan.order`. Document that the first failure named is the first by that order.
  E7 [low] P1 is confirmed but the ADR understates it. `Array.sort()` and `<` on `StringName` are not lexical (reproduced on a 14-id set: `[layout, graph, sanity.perception, ... body]`). `Array[StringName].sort()` gives the identical wrong order. The result depends on interning order: the same four names created in the reverse order sorted alphabetically. That points to a pointer or intern-order compare, so it can differ between builds, platforms and hosts, not just between runs. The ADR says 'stable across two runs', which is the weaker framing, and ADR-0005 P12 already states it correctly. `StringName < StringName` also passes the analyzer (only mixed `StringName` against `String` is a parse error), so RST-01 must be type-aware and the compiler will not catch it. The `String(a) < String(b)` remedy is correct (code-point order, alphabetical in the probe). RST-01 overlaps the existing ADR-0005 AST rule 'StringName passed to sort()'.
    amendment: In P1 cite ADR-0005 P12 and say 'order depends on interning order; may differ between builds, platforms and hosts'. Make RST-01 a member of the ADR-0005 or DET lint rather than a parallel rule, with `<` and `>` added to its operand check. Note that KRN-RST-06 must pick ids whose interning order differs from alphabetical, including creating them in reverse order, because the bug is allocation-dependent.
  E8 [low] KRN-RST-05 uses a 'seeded shuffle of ready lists'. `Array.shuffle()` and `randi` use the global RNG, which is banned by DET-01 in sim and kernel. In the test tree it would make the order-permutation test non-reproducible or tied to global seeding. Separately, `RestorePlan` exposes its results as public `var order/rank/world_order/post_order/bind_order: PackedInt32Array`. They are reference types (see E3), so any holder can write through `plan.order[i] = x`. 4.7 element writes call no setter, so nothing intercepts it. The ADR calls the plan 'immutable'. The language has no readonly.
    amendment: Build the shuffled linear extensions with a test-owned Fisher-Yates driven by `DetRng` (ADR-0005), never `Array.shuffle()`. Make the plan fields private (`_order` and so on) and expose `order_at(i)`, `rank_of(index)` and `size()`. Or hand out `.duplicate()` copies and keep the immutability claim to 'immutable by convention, checked by hash of `describe()`'.
  
  ADR-0016 review verdict CONCERNS:
  T1 [High, BLOCKING] The Interaction subject repair rests on an assumption that ADR-0017 contradicts. ADR-0016 rates TR-interact-016 'Covered with a GDD sync' by assuming Interaction's repair hook runs before emitter.place (its cross-ADR assumption on ADR-0017 and its Open Question 5). ADR-0017 D2.5, D6.1 and its ADR-0020 row order the Interaction hook AFTER emitter.place and accept a one-tick lag. ADR-0017 D10.2 also has registrants 're-register idempotently in their own post_restore (restore_after allows it)'. ADR-0016 § 4.2, Alternative 6 and ADR-0003 § 4 forbid exactly that: open_for(emitter.state) in a RESTORE scope is REFUSED and counted as WRITE_OUTSIDE_SCOPE. The IA-36 GDD sync string ADR-0016 hands the orchestrator would therefore promise an ordering no sibling provides.
    amendment: Close Open Question 5 in ADR-0016 with this model. Subject registrations are persisted. post_restore only detects drift (V10, IA_RESTORE_SUBJECT_DRIFT). The repair is Interaction's ordinary hook rule, which ADR-0017 orders after emitter.place, so the table reflects the repair at the next emitter.place (a lag of one tick at most). G4 is unaffected because a consistent save has empty drift. Downgrade TR-interact-016 to Partial (the repair timing is ADR-0020's). Reword the IA-36 sync to: 'post_restore re-registers nothing; drift is detected there and repaired by the first Interaction hook run, reflected at the following emitter.place'. Remove 'emitter.place is ordered after the Interaction hook' from the assumptions.
  T2 [High, BLOCKING] The hook-cursor verifier that ADR-0012 hands to ADR-0016 is missing from the § 5.3 list, and § 3.2 forbids it. ADR-0012 (§ 1, its TR-lsg-023 row and its ADR-0016 assumption) says ADR-0016's restore verifier checks each last_step_X against the restored clock. V3 and V4 do not list that check, and § 3.2 says restore 'never reads kernel.clock T for a decision', so a verifier that faults on T is barred. § 5.1 calls § 5.3 the single numbered list of cross-block checks, so a check absent from it has no slot and no KRN-RST-12 fixture.
    amendment: In § 3.4, add kernel.clock (T, world_seed) as Tier S from R2 onward. restore_epoch stays readable only inside RngFacet.draw_epoch, per ADR-0003 § 10. Reword § 3.2 as: 'never derives simulation state from T; a structural verifier may compare persisted stamps with T'. Add to V3/V4: 'each Graph hook cursor last_step_X equals the step of the last tick at or before T on which hook X was due (ADR-0012 § 1, step-0 convention); fault GRAPH_RESTORE_HOOK_CURSOR (local 25 per ADR-0012)'. Add a KRN-RST-12 fixture row for it.
  T3 [Medium, BLOCKING] The StringName ordering fence duplicates the Foundation rules and conflicts with them. ADR-0005 P12 already probed that StringName sort is not lexical, and the registry already holds the forbidden pattern stringname_sort_for_canonical_order. The ADR-0010 DET pack bans .sort_custom( in src/kernel/ and states that StringName sorting is not lexically decidable; the only allowed forms are CanonicalEncoder.sorted_string_keys and sorted_int_keys. ADR-0016 instead proposes BlockIdOrder.less as a comparator (src/shared/block_id_order.gd), which implies sort_custom in the kernel. It also proposes RST-01 as a type-aware lexical rule, a new forbidden pattern 'stringname_ordering', and lists 'a real engine trap found' as a positive consequence.
    amendment: Drop BlockIdOrder and RST-01. Build bind_order once at the freeze through ADR-0005's sanctioned helper: CanonicalEncoder.sorted_string_keys, or Array[String].assign(ids) followed by sort(). Map the result back to registration indices. Cite stringname_sort_for_canonical_order and the DET pack, and add ADR-0016 to that pattern's referenced_by instead of a new pattern. Keep P1 as corroboration of ADR-0005 P12 and remove the 'trap found' claim from Positive consequences.
  T4 [Medium, BLOCKING] The acceptance gate cannot be met as stated. Verification (1) gates acceptance on KRN-RST-05 green on the KRN-LAT-02 headless stub skeleton. § 8 defines KRN-RST-05 over a seeded world with a read-view battery (lit, top_emitter, room_at, served_pm, door-leaf rects, seat bindings), which needs implemented Layout, Graph, Emitter and Body blocks: Migration Plan stories 5 and 6, which are blocked while those ADRs are Proposed. The architecture § Spikes table also does not list ADR-0016 under KRN-LAT-02, so the gate is invisible to spike planning.
    amendment: Gate acceptance on KRN-RST-01, -02 and -04 plus a stub-level KRN-RST-05. The stub version runs recorded stub blocks with the MVP restore_after edges. A planted stub that reads a non-predecessor's Tier D state must diverge under at least one of the four linear extensions, and a stub that respects its edges must match under all four. Move the real-world battery to a Save/Load or Kernel epic closure gate. Add an ADR-0016 row to architecture.md § Spikes that gate ADRs (KRN-LAT-02 build).
  T5 [Medium] Key Interfaces are not concrete enough for stories. (a) load_stage.gd declares two class_names (LoadStage and LoadFailure); GDScript allows one per file, and ADR-0003 § 6 practice is one class per file. (b) KRN-RST-05 must replace the RestorePlan with alternative linear extensions, but the plan is immutable and exposes only compile(), so there is no test seam. (c) The cold-open pass that visits PROFILE blocks has no pass-kind input on request_restore. (d) ADR-0002 also calls binding sources during RUNNING (STRICT_DEBUG BINDING_DRIFT), yet § 6.2 describes them only as running after every post_restore.
    amendment: Move LoadFailure to src/kernel/load_failure.gd. Add a test seam: RestorePlan.from_order(order: PackedInt32Array, blocks, out_errors), which validates that the order is a linear extension of the DAG, or compile(blocks, max_blocks, tie_break: int, seed: int, out_errors). State that the pass kind (IN_SESSION or COLD_OPEN) is deferred to the first PROFILE block, or add it to the request. Reword § 6.2 so a binding_source is a pure read valid at any boundary, not only after post_restore.
  T6 [Medium] The H1 allow-list extension and the foundation-ask list are incomplete. RestorePlan (registries), LoadFailure and LoadTiming (diagnostics) are new kernel members. ADR-0003 § 10 says the H1 lint's fixed list is 'extended by exactly these names', but no ask is filed for them. Negative consequences count 'five foundation changes (three kernel codes, two pass codes, an outcome record)', while the ADR adds four codes (18 to 21), a boot warning and an outcome record. The ADR-0003 § 9 triggers load_done and load_failed, which R7 and the fault path must fire, are not named.
    amendment: Add an ADR-0003 § 10 foundation ask naming restore_plan (registries) and load_failure and load_timing (diagnostics). Correct the count in Negative consequences to match the Key Interfaces list. In § 1.1 and § 1.3, name the transitions: R7 fires load_done, and any pass fault fires load_failed.
  T7 [Low] The pre-check's first failure is not deterministic. R1 (a) and (d) walk the payload Dictionary. When two blocks are bad, the block that gets named depends on Dictionary iteration order, against § 2.2 ('Dictionary iteration never decides anything') and § 5.5's deterministic first failure. Check (a) also does not say how the kernel.clock payload key is handled; ADR-0006 § 3.6 puts it in the payload.
    amendment: R1 (a) walks payload keys in ascending String order and treats kernel.clock as known. R1 (d) walks RestorePlan.world_order. Add one KRN-RST-03 case with two bad blocks.
  T8 [Low] The Tier S/D tag lint does not exist, and the stale_* obligation is wide. § 3.4 and Risk R2 say a lint 'of the same pack' reads the Tier S/D doc tags, but RST-01 to RST-04 contain no such rule. § 3.4 also requires every Tier D getter of every block to return a neutral value and raise a stale_* diagnostic, which is a lot of boilerplate for a solo or small team.
    amendment: Either add RST-05 ('every public method of a src/sim/*/views/*_view.gd carries ## @tier S or ## @tier D') or drop the lint claim and name KRN-RST-05 as the only check. Limit the stale_* obligation to Tier D getters that a verifier or another block actually reads during the pass.
  T9 [Low] § 4.4 says the stock reconcile runs 'at the head of phase 0 of the first Graph step'. That reads as a first-run rule, which § 4.3 forbids; ADR-0011 § 7.3 says 'the head of every phase 0'. KRN-RST-13's 'verdict MATCH except the documented phase-0 clamp' is also confusing, because the verdict is computed at R5, before any step runs.
    amendment: Reword § 4.4 as: 'at the head of every phase 0 (a no-op in steady state); the first step after a load is simply the first that can find a store above the live cap'. KRN-RST-13: 'verdict MATCH in every case; the phase-0 clamp is asserted on the first step's stock_clamped and diagnostic'.
  
  CROSS-ADR RULINGS (binding):
  CT-01 owner ADR-0011 (align: ADR-0013, ADR-0012, ADR-0016): Merges 0011-review items 1 (first half) and 7, 0013-review items 1 and 9, and ADR-0011 T4. ADR-0013 owns the `LayoutGraphPort` definition. ADR-0011 is the implementer and currently publishes nothing for it. The Graph facade cannot be `GraphModule` or `GraphView`: GDScript has single inheritance, and `GraphView` must stay a pure, getter-only view. The implementer therefore has to be a dedicated adapter class. It cannot sit under `ports/`, because ADR-0010 ARCH-05 requires every file under `ports/` to be `@abstract`. The out-type name is the port owner's: `SectionBases` wins, and `InstantiateResult` is deleted, not aliased. M1's call chain follows ADR-0013 (Web Map -> LM1 -> port), because Layout allocates `section_id` first.
    amendment: ADR-0011, new section 9.5 'Layout port' plus a Key Interfaces snippet: `class_name GraphLayoutAdapter extends LayoutGraphPort` in `src/sim/graph/graph_layout_adapter.gd` (outside `ports/`, ARCH-05). GraphModule.setup constructs it and exposes it as `graph.layout_port()`. It holds `GraphMutators` and `GraphView`, so `GraphView` keeps its pure getter-only contract. It implements all five methods with caller-owned outs and no allocation: (1) `check_instantiate_section(views, section_id: int, template_id: String, kind: int) -> StringName`, the pure Class A check returning the LS-18 reasons plus CAPACITY and ONSET_UNKEYED, which is the same function ADR-0012 calls `check_instantiate_section`; (2) `instantiate_section(scope, section_id, template_id, kind, out: SectionBases) -> int`, which is M1; (3) `opening_into(edge_id, out: OpeningRead) -> bool`, with `door_state` derived from `area` (LS-19); (4) `seam_openings_into(seam_id, out: SeamOpenings) -> bool`, with `opening_ids` in `socket_plan.openings` order and valid after restore; (5) `section_counts_into(section_id, out: SectionCounts) -> bool`, which reads persisted columns only (Tier S) and follows CT-03. The reads are valid in APPLY, INIT, HOOK and post_restore. The two writers are valid in APPLY and INIT. Delete `views/instantiate_result.gd`. M1's out type is ADR-0013's `SectionBases {node_base, edge_base, comp_base}` (in `src/sim/layout/views/`). Update section 11 and the interfaces registry candidate to match. In the section 1 row 'init_world, binding_source' and in section 4.4, write: 'M1's only caller is Layout LM1 through `LayoutGraphPort`; LM1's callers are those ADR-0013 section 9 names (Web Map `init_world` in the INIT scope at the MVP).' ADR-0012 section 6 (M1 row and Rules) gets the same wording. ADR-0016 section 3.4's Tier S list already names these reads and needs no change.
  CT-03 owner ADR-0011 (align: ADR-0013, ADR-0016): Merges 0013-review item 10 and ADR-0013 T2. A RAGGED cut appends STUB HULL_SEGMENT rows with fresh high ids outside the section's contiguous M1 range. Discard tombstones the whole range. `section_counts_into` must define both cases, or every save made after a RAGGED cut fails Layout's post_restore check (d).
    amendment: ADR-0011 section 9.5 (CT-01): `section_counts_into(section_id, out)` fills the template-range counts, which are the rows in `[node_base, node_base + template.node_count)` and the matching edge range that M1 created for this section, and the compartments `comp_base + k`. It also fills `stub_count`, the STUB rows a RAGGED `cut_detach` created; a stub's `section_of` is the cut section, and stubs are outside the template range. It sets `tombstoned` true when every template-range row of the section is tombstoned (a discarded section). Sections 3.6 and 4.1 (3) cite this. ADR-0013 section 10 (d): for each non-discarded instance, the template-range rows resolve to section s and are not tombstoned, and compartment k equals `comp_base + k`. Rows outside the template range (stubs, seam edges) are excluded. For a discarded instance, the same ranges resolve to tombstones of s. ADR-0013 section 3: the bsearch reverse lookup over `node_base` covers template-range ids only. Stub ids resolve through `GraphView.section_of(id)` plus the seam's stub list, and `anchor_geometry(stub)` answers the cut socket's hatch span. Add a fixture: RAGGED cut, save, restore, the verifier passes, and `anchor_geometry(stub)` is as specified. ADR-0016 V2 is reworded to 'template-range counts match; stubs and seam edges excluded'.
  CT-04 owner ADR-0011 (align: ADR-0012, ADR-0017, ADR-0016, ADR-0022): Merges 0011-review items 2 and 4, 0012-review item 4(1), 0016-review item 7 (delta_w_last5) and ADR-0011 T1. The request is accepted. ADR-0012 section 11 shows that a restore landing between the power hook and the atmo or failure hook cannot rebuild `served`, `draw` or the cable net load from post-phase state. That is a real G4 divergence, and Alternative 7 does not answer it. The same argument covers the five-step `power_use` window that ADR-0012 seeds flat. Attention consumes that window, and KRN-RST-05 allows no exception list, so the window is persisted too. ADR-0012 T2 option (a), which recomputes the intensive caches at the end of phase 0, keeps P, p_o2, o2_pm and trend DERIVED and exact. The `stock_cap` reconcile already agrees with ADR-0016 section 4.4.
    amendment: ADR-0011: (a) section 3.2 adds node columns `n_served` (int32, permille) and `n_draw` (int32, dJ per step), with canonical zero on every node that is not a power consumer and range specs in `GraphSchema`. (b) Section 3.4 defines `e0` of a CABLE edge as its net load in W, with a stated sign convention and min/max. (c) Section 3.8 hdr adds `power_use_w5` (five int ints, the ADR-0012 `delta_w_last5` window). (d) The section 6.1 PERSISTED row adds 'hook products: n_served, n_draw, CABLE e0 (written by ADR-0012 phase 2 only), power_use_w5'. `served_pm` moves out of DERIVED: it is read from `n_served`. (e) Section 7.4 (3) reads: 'post_restore re-derives P, p_o2, o2_pm and trend, and never served or draw.' (f) Rewrite Alternative 7 so it rejects persisting only the intensive atmosphere values, and cite ADR-0012 section 11 for the hook products. (g) Update section 3.11, Risks 1, the performance_budgets candidate and the Validation size line to about 30.5 KB (plus 40 bytes) with about 4.6 percent headroom. (h) Remove `served_pm` from the `derived_members.json` description. (i) Add GDD sync items for LS-21, LS-4 and the TR-lsg-004 wording. (j) Close Open Question 2: the phase-0 stock reconcile is agreed with ADR-0016 section 4.4. ADR-0012 section 11 and ADR-0017 D14.4 delete their 'if ADR-0011 declines' fallback text. ADR-0012 section 11 deletes the 'power_use window seeded flat' accepted divergence and restores the window from `power_use_w5`.
  CT-05 owner ADR-0011 (align: ADR-0012, ADR-0017, ADR-0016): Merges 0011-review item 5, 0012-review item 4(2) and ADR-0011 T2. ADR-0012 section 1 owns the hook cursors and defines `last_step_no` as the last step whose failure hook completed (LS-8). ADR-0017's FAULT_GLOW reconcile and FT-15 depend on that meaning. ADR-0011 adopts it.
    amendment: ADR-0011 section 2.3, last sentence: '`hdr.last_step_no` is the last step whose failure hook (phase 11) completed (LS-8, ADR-0012 section 1). It trails `step_no()` by up to one step, and equals it only from the end of the failure hook until the next power-hook tick.' Section 3.8's hdr list and the `GraphView.last_step_no()` doc comment say the same.
  CT-08 owner ADR-0011 (align: ADR-0012, ADR-0016): Merges 0011-review item 8, 0012-review item 5, 0016-review item 6 and ADR-0016 T2. The Graph owns its fault table and restore steps, so the cursor check belongs in ADR-0011 section 7.2, and ADR-0016 V3 covers it by reference. ADR-0016 section 3.2 currently bars any read of T in restore, so it must allow a structural comparison with T. The hook offsets are GraphTuning, and ADR-0016 section 4.4 forbids asserting a catalogue tunable at restore. The cursors are therefore checked against offsets stored in the payload, which is a structural, byte-identical comparison. A schedule change across a save is handled at the first hook run, not at restore. Local codes: 25 is the runtime HOOK_CURSOR that ADR-0012 raises, and 26 is the restore check. The reviewers' 'GRAPH_RESTORE_HOOK_CURSOR local 25' collides with the runtime code and is renumbered to 26.
    amendment: ADR-0011: section 3.8 hdr adds `sched` (four ints: GRAPH_STEP_TICKS and `hook_offset_power/atmo/failure` in force when the cursors were written). Section 8.1 appends `25 HOOK_CURSOR` (runtime, raised by ADR-0012 section 1) and `26 RESTORE_HOOK_CURSOR`. # Global instructions (all projects)

## Dynamic Workflows: model choice

- Always use Sonnet 5.5 (`model: 'sonnet'`) or Haiku (`model: 'haiku'`) for worker agents in Dynamic Workflows (the Workflow tool's `agent()` calls), to preserve token usage. Use Haiku for mechanical stages (logging, formatting, simple extraction) and Sonnet for the rest.
- Opus or Fable is acceptable only as an advisor where needed: a senior reviewer, judge or verdict seat, never for bulk work such as planners, writers, fixers or scanners.
- Set `model` explicitly on every worker `agent()` call; do not let workers inherit the session model.

# Claude Code Game Studios -- Game Studio Agent Architecture

Indie game development managed through 49 coordinated Claude Code subagents.
Each agent owns a specific domain, enforcing separation of concerns and quality.

## Technology Stack

- **Engine**: Godot 4.7.2
- **Language**: GDScript
- **Version Control**: Git with trunk-based development
- **Build System**: SCons (engine), Godot Export Templates
- **Asset Pipeline**: Godot Import System + custom resource pipeline

> **Note**: Engine-specialist agents exist for Godot, Unity, and Unreal with
> dedicated sub-specialists. Use the set matching your engine.

## Project Structure

@.claude/docs/directory-structure.md

## Engine Version Reference

@docs/engine-reference/godot/VERSION.md


## Technical Preferences

`project.yaml` at the repo root is the primary config store — engine, specialists,
naming, platform, performance, modes. Skills resolve it via `resolve_config`
(see `.claude/docs/config-resolution.md`).

`.claude/docs/technical-preferences.md` is the **legacy fallback**, read on demand
when a key is absent from `project.yaml`. It is not imported here: before
`/setup-engine` runs it is almost entirely `[TO BE CONFIGURED]` placeholders, and
after it runs `project.yaml` holds the real values.

## Coordination Rules

@.claude/docs/coordination-rules.md

## Collaboration Protocol

**User-driven collaboration, not autonomous execution.**
Every task follows: **Question -> Options -> Decision -> Draft -> Approval**

- Agents MUST ask "May I write this to [filepath]?" before using Write/Edit tools
  (exempt: `active.md` appends, agent memory, a subagent's new file at the path
  its orchestrating skill named; see `.claude/rules/agent-memory.md`)
- Agents MUST show drafts or summaries before requesting approval
- Multi-file changes require explicit approval for the full changeset
- No commits without user instruction
- A skipped or dismissed question is not an answer: act on nothing, re-ask in
  plain text and wait
- Started outside this file's folder? Warn first: hooks, deny rules and the
  ask-first mode load only when Claude Code starts here

See `docs/COLLABORATIVE-DESIGN-PRINCIPLE.md` for full protocol and examples.

> **First session?** If the project has no engine configured and no game concept,
> run `/start` to begin the guided onboarding flow.

## Coding Standards

@.claude/docs/coding-standards.md

## Context Management

Read `.claude/docs/context-management.md` on demand — it is a reference, not
session context. Two of its conventions are load-bearing and cited by name
elsewhere in the repo, so they are restated here rather than lost:

- **`production/session-state/active.md` is the session checkpoint.** The file is
  the memory, not the conversation. Read it first after any compaction, crash, or
  `/clear`.
- **Helpers in `.claude/scripts/` emit observations, never verdicts.** A script
  that scores or judges will eventually contradict a mode or override it cannot
  see. (Cited by `artifact-check.sh` and `adr-dep-graph.sh`.)

# Directory Structure

```text
/
├── CLAUDE.md                    # Master configuration
├── project.yaml                 # Machine-readable project config — engine, modes, stage (source of truth)
├── .claude/                     # Agent definitions, skills, hooks, rules, docs
├── <code root>/                 # Game source code — THE PATH IS ENGINE-SPECIFIC, see below
├── assets/                      # Game assets (art, audio, vfx, shaders, data)
├── design/                      # Game design documents (gdd, narrative, levels, balance)
├── docs/                        # Technical documentation (architecture, api, postmortems)
│   └── engine-reference/        # Curated engine API snapshots (version-pinned)
├── tests/                       # Game test suites (unit, integration, performance, playtest)
├── tools/                       # Build and pipeline tools (ci, build, asset-pipeline)
├── prototypes/                  # Throwaway prototypes (outside the code root)
├── production/                  # Production management (sprints, milestones, releases)
│   ├── session-state/           # Ephemeral session state (active.md — gitignored)
│   └── session-logs/            # Session audit trail (gitignored)
└── studio-tests/                # QA for the skills/agents themselves — /skill-test, /skill-improve
```

## The code root is engine-specific

**Two of the three supported engines will not build a project whose code sits in
`src/`.** This is not a style preference — it is a hard constraint of the engine's
own toolchain:

| `engine.name` | Code root | Why it cannot be `src/` |
|---|---|---|
| **Godot** | `src/` | No constraint — Godot loads from `res://` anywhere under the project root. |
| **Unity** | `Assets/` | Unity compiles **only** `Assets/` and `Packages/`. Code outside them is invisible to the compiler. |
| **Unreal** | `Source/<Module>/` | UnrealBuildTool discovers modules under `Source/`; content lives in `Content/`. A module elsewhere is not built. |

**Resolve the code root from `engine.name` before writing any source file.** A
path shown as `src/…` alone is a Godot example: read it as *"the code root"* and
substitute the row above. `src/` is the table's Godot row, not a universal path.

**Tests follow the same rule** — the same compilers decide what they see:

| `engine.name` | Test root | Anywhere else |
|---|---|---|
| **Godot** | `tests/unit/`, `tests/integration/` | — |
| **Unity** | `Assets/Tests/EditMode/`, `Assets/Tests/PlayMode/` | not compiled: "0 tests, Passed" |
| **Unreal** | `Source/<Module>/Private/Tests/` | not built: "No automation tests matched" |

Read `tests/unit/[system]/` (or `integration/`) anywhere as the test root plus `[System]/`.

# Godot Engine — Version Reference

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Engine Version** | Godot 4.7 |
| **Installed at pin time** | 4.7.2.stable.mono.official.ed1daf0bf (matches pin; probed 2026-10-25 at `C:/Users/dasbl/Documents/Godot/`). 4.6.2 standard is also installed, unused. |
| **Release Date** | June 2026 (latest patch: 4.7.2, August 2026) |
| **Project Pinned** | 2026-10-17 |
| **Last Docs Verified** | 2026-10-17 (release timeline and 4.7 changes); 2026-02-12 (4.4-4.6 content) |
| **LLM Knowledge Cutoff** | May 2025 |

## Knowledge Gap Warning

The LLM's training data likely covers Godot up to ~4.3. Versions 4.5, 4.6
and 4.7 were released after the cutoff and introduced significant changes that
the model does NOT know about; 4.4 came out shortly before it and may be thinly
covered. Always cross-reference this directory before suggesting Godot API calls.

## Installed-Version Gap Warning

The warning above is one-directional — it covers the **model** knowing less than
this pin. The reverse gap is real and `/setup-engine` §3 creates it deliberately
("pin the newer one and upgrade later"): this reference can sit **ahead of the
installed editor**, and an agent citing it correctly then emits APIs that do not
compile locally. **Check `Installed at pin time` above before trusting a
version-qualified claim** — `NOT DETERMINED` means the gap is unknown, not absent.

## Post-Cutoff Version Timeline

| Version | Release | Risk Level | Key Theme |
|---------|---------|------------|-----------|
| 4.5 | Sep 2025 | HIGH | Accessibility (AccessKit), variadic args, @abstract, shader baker, SMAA |
| 4.6 | Jan 2026 | HIGH | Jolt default, glow rework, D3D12 default on Windows, IK restored |
| 4.7 | Jun 2026 | HIGH | AreaLight3D, HDR output, Asset Store replaces the Asset Library, VirtualJoystick, Jolt soft-body and world-boundary changes, typed-return overrides |

## Before the Cutoff

4.4 (Mar 2025, Jolt option, FileAccess return types) predates the May 2025
cutoff; the Knowledge Gap Warning still applies to it.

Dates from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/releases, checked 2026-10-17:
4.4 Mar 3 2025, 4.5 Sep 15 2025, 4.6 Jan 26 2026, 4.7 Jun 18 2026, 4.7.2 Aug 18
2026. Migration guides and release notes: `breaking-changes.md` § Sources.

# Agent Coordination Rules

1. **Vertical Delegation**: Leadership agents delegate to department leads, who
   delegate to specialists. Never skip a tier for complex decisions.
2. **Horizontal Consultation**: Agents at the same tier may consult each other
   but must not make binding decisions outside their domain.
3. **Conflict Resolution**: When two agents disagree, escalate to the shared
   parent. If no shared parent, escalate to `creative-director` for design
   conflicts or `technical-director` for technical conflicts.
4. **Change Propagation**: When a design change affects multiple domains, the
   `producer` agent coordinates the propagation.
5. **No Unilateral Cross-Domain Changes**: An agent must never modify files
   outside its designated directories without explicit delegation.
6. **Read Design Docs by Section**: A brief names the sections an agent needs
   by heading. Find a heading in a GDD, ADR or the art bible with the Grep
   tool (`^#`, content mode) and Read that range with offset and limit; read a doc
   whole only when the task needs all of it, and say why. `validate-read.sh`
   refuses a whole-file read of a doc over 40 KB.
7. **Nothing Goes Upstream**: Never file, open or comment on an issue or pull
   request in an engine, plugin or vendor repository, even when asked. Write a
   draft (`/bug-report` drafts only) and the user submits it.

## Model Tier Assignment

Read `.claude/docs/model-tiers.md` on demand. It carries the tier table, the
per-skill assignments and the authoring rule.

**Key point:** whether a skill's `model:` is used
depends on how the skill starts. Typed as `/skill-name`: yes, except a `haiku`
pin in auto mode. Started by Claude through the Skill tool: no. Never tell a
user a `haiku` skill saves money; an `opus` skill typed in a Sonnet session
costs more. The agent-side `model:` is a different mechanism, and is applied.

## Subagents vs Agent Teams

This project uses two distinct multi-agent patterns:

### Subagents (current, always active)
Spawned via the `Agent` tool within a single Claude Code session. Used by all
`team-*` skills and orchestration skills. Subagents share the session's
permission context, run sequentially or in parallel within the session, and
return results to the parent.

**When to spawn in parallel**: If two subagents' inputs are independent (neither
needs the other's output to begin), spawn both `Agent` calls simultaneously
rather than waiting. Example: `/review-all-gdds` **Phase 2** (consistency) and
**Phase 3** (design theory) are independent — spawn both at the same time.
Phase 1 loads the GDDs and both depend on it, so it is the one phase here that
must NOT be parallelised.

### Agent Teams (experimental — opt-in)
Multiple independent Claude Code *sessions* coordinated via a shared task list.
Opt-in only — read `.claude/docs/agent-teams.md` on demand before proposing one.

## Parallel Task Protocol

When an orchestration skill spawns multiple independent agents:

1. Issue all independent `Agent` calls before waiting for any result
2. Collect all results before proceeding to dependent phases
3. If any agent is BLOCKED, surface it immediately — do not silently skip
4. Always produce a partial report if some agents complete and others block

# Coding Standards

- All game code must include doc comments on public APIs
- Architecture decisions are recorded as ADRs in `docs/architecture/`. **How many is
  set by `modes.workflow`** — all ADRs at `full`, *critical* ADRs only at `standard`,
  and none required at `minimal`, where the decision log and `design/game-brief.md`
  carry the rationale instead. See `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.
- Gameplay values must be data-driven (external config), never hardcoded
- All public methods must be unit-testable (dependency injection over singletons)
- Commits must reference the relevant design document or task ID
- **Commit messages**: Use Conventional Commits format — `feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, `test:`, `refactor:`. Reference the story or task ID in the body (e.g., `Story: EPIC-001-S02`).
- **Verification-driven development**: Write tests first when adding gameplay systems.
  For UI changes, verify with screenshots. Compare expected output to actual output
  before marking work complete. Every implementation should have a way to prove it works.
- **A parse check is not a run.** Every story that changes something
  player-observable is launched and observed before it closes, and the
  observation is a retained screenshot in `production/qa/evidence/`. Procedure
  per engine: `.claude/docs/run-and-observe.md`. Not waived at
  `qa.level: minimal` — tests are, the look is not.

# Design Document Standards

- All design docs use Markdown
- Each mechanic has a dedicated document in `design/gdd/`
- **How many of the 8 sections are required depends on `modes.workflow`** —
  all 8 at `full`, 5 (+ Formulas when the system defines numeric rules — rates,
  curves, thresholds, costs; the system's `Category` is a hint, not the test) at
  `standard`, and no
  GDD at all at `minimal`, where `design/game-brief.md` is the design record.
  See `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`. The 8 sections:
  1. **Overview** -- one-paragraph summary
  2. **Player Fantasy** -- intended feeling and experience
  3. **Detailed Rules** -- unambiguous mechanics
  4. **Formulas** -- all math defined with variables
  5. **Edge Cases** -- unusual situations handled
  6. **Dependencies** -- other systems listed
  7. **Tuning Knobs** -- configurable values identified
  8. **Acceptance Criteria** -- testable success conditions
- Balance values must link to their source formula or rationale

# Testing Standards

## Test Evidence by Story Type

All stories must have appropriate test evidence before they can be marked Done:

| Story Type | Required Evidence | Location | Default Gate Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Logic** (formulas, AI, state machines) | Automated unit test — must pass | `tests/unit/[system]/` | BLOCKING |
| **Integration** (multi-system) | Integration test OR documented playtest | `tests/integration/[system]/` | BLOCKING |
| **Visual/Feel** (animation, VFX, feel) | Retained screenshot + lead sign-off | `production/qa/evidence/` | BLOCKING |
| **UI** (menus, HUD, screens) | Retained screenshot of each screen touched | `production/qa/evidence/` | BLOCKING |
| **Config/Data** (balance tuning) | Smoke check pass | `production/qa/smoke-[date].md` | ADVISORY |

The **Default Gate Level** applies when `testing.strict` is not set in
`project.yaml`. A project may override it per test type: `testing.strict.logic`,
`.integration`, `.visual`, `.ui`, and `.config` each take `true` (BLOCKING) or
`false` (ADVISORY). `/story-done`, `/story-readiness`, `/dev-story`,
`/gate-check`, and `/smoke-check` resolve the effective level from that setting,
falling back to the defaults above when it is absent.

> **Why Visual and UI block.** "Retained" is load-bearing — the screenshot must
> still be on disk in `production/qa/evidence/` when the story is closed. One
> that was captured and discarded is an assertion, not evidence. These two rows
> block because for a game the way it looks *is* the product: an advisory visual
> gate gets deferred in favour of whatever does block, and the result is a
> well-tested game that looks wrong.

> **Exception — `/smoke-check`.** The ADVISORY default for **Config/Data** above
> applies to *per-story evidence* gates. `/smoke-check` is a build-health gate,
> not a per-story evidence gate, so its own unset default for
> `testing.strict.config` is **BLOCKING**. The two defaults differ on purpose.

## Automated Test Rules

- **Naming**: per engine — `.claude/rules/test-standards.md`
- **Determinism**: Tests must produce the same result every run — no random seeds, no time-dependent assertions
- **Isolation**: Each test sets up and tears down its own state; tests must not depend on execution order
- **No hardcoded data**: Test fixtures use constant files or factory functions, not inline magic numbers
  (exception: boundary value tests where the exact number IS the point)
- **Independence**: Unit tests do not call external APIs, databases, or file I/O — use dependency injection

## What NOT to Automate

- Visual fidelity (shader output, VFX appearance, animation curves)
- "Feel" qualities (input responsiveness, perceived weight, timing)
- Platform-specific rendering (test on target hardware, not headlessly)
- Full gameplay sessions (covered by playtesting, not automation)

## CI/CD Rules

- Automated test suite runs on every push to main and every PR
- No merge if tests fail — tests are a blocking gate in CI
- Never disable or skip failing tests to make CI pass — fix the underlying issue
- Engine-specific CI commands:
  - **Godot**: `godot --headless -s -d --remote-debug tcp://127.0.0.1:0 res://addons/gdUnit4/bin/GdUnitCmdTool.gd -a res://tests --ignoreHeadlessMode`
  - **Unity**: `game-ci/unity-test-runner@v4` (GitHub Actions)
  - **Unreal**: headless runner with `-nullrhi` flag
- [Consistency-check needs a confirming run](consistency-check-confirming-run.md) — owner+registry fixes leave leftovers in consumer GDDs; grep referenced_by docs, print patch counts

**Resolve the code root from `engine.name` before writing any source file.** A
path shown as `src/…` alone is a Godot example: read it as *"the code root"* and
substitute the row above. `src/` is the table's Godot row, not a universal path.

**Tests follow the same rule** — the same compilers decide what they see:

| `engine.name` | Test root | Anywhere else |
|---|---|---|
| **Godot** | `tests/unit/`, `tests/integration/` | — |
| **Unity** | `Assets/Tests/EditMode/`, `Assets/Tests/PlayMode/` | not compiled: "0 tests, Passed" |
| **Unreal** | `Source/<Module>/Private/Tests/` | not built: "No automation tests matched" |

Read `tests/unit/[system]/` (or `integration/`) anywhere as the test root plus `[System]/`.

# Agent Coordination Rules

1. **Vertical Delegation**: Leadership agents delegate to department leads, who
   delegate to specialists. Never skip a tier for complex decisions.
2. **Horizontal Consultation**: Agents at the same tier may consult each other
   but must not make binding decisions outside their domain.
3. **Conflict Resolution**: When two agents disagree, escalate to the shared
   parent. If no shared parent, escalate to `creative-director` for design
   conflicts or `technical-director` for technical conflicts.
4. **Change Propagation**: When a design change affects multiple domains, the
   `producer` agent coordinates the propagation.
5. **No Unilateral Cross-Domain Changes**: An agent must never modify files
   outside its designated directories without explicit delegation.
6. **Read Design Docs by Section**: A brief names the sections an agent needs
   by heading. Find a heading in a GDD, ADR or the art bible with the Grep
   tool (`^#`, content mode) and Read that range with offset and limit; read a doc
   whole only when the task needs all of it, and say why. `validate-read.sh`
   refuses a whole-file read of a doc over 40 KB.
7. **Nothing Goes Upstream**: Never file, open or comment on an issue or pull
   request in an engine, plugin or vendor repository, even when asked. Write a
   draft (`/bug-report` drafts only) and the user submits it.

## Model Tier Assignment

Read `.claude/docs/model-tiers.md` on demand. It carries the tier table, the
per-skill assignments and the authoring rule.

**Key point:** whether a skill's `model:` is used
depends on how the skill starts. Typed as `/skill-name`: yes, except a `haiku`
pin in auto mode. Started by Claude through the Skill tool: no. Never tell a
user a `haiku` skill saves money; an `opus` skill typed in a Sonnet session
costs more. The agent-side `model:` is a different mechanism, and is applied.

## Subagents vs Agent Teams

This project uses two distinct multi-agent patterns:

### Subagents (current, always active)
Spawned via the `Agent` tool within a single Claude Code session. Used by all
`team-*` skills and orchestration skills. Subagents share the session's
permission context, run sequentially or in parallel within the session, and
return results to the parent.

**When to spawn in parallel**: If two subagents' inputs are independent (neither
needs the other's output to begin), spawn both `Agent` calls simultaneously
rather than waiting. Example: `/review-all-gdds` **Phase 2** (consistency) and
**Phase 3** (design theory) are independent — spawn both at the same time.
Phase 1 loads the GDDs and both depend on it, so it is the one phase here that
must NOT be parallelised.

### Agent Teams (experimental — opt-in)
Multiple independent Claude Code *sessions* coordinated via a shared task list.
Opt-in only — read `.claude/docs/agent-teams.md` on demand before proposing one.

## Parallel Task Protocol

When an orchestration skill spawns multiple independent agents:

1. Issue all independent `Agent` calls before waiting for any result
2. Collect all results before proceeding to dependent phases
3. If any agent is BLOCKED, surface it immediately — do not silently skip
4. Always produce a partial report if some agents complete and others block

# Coding Standards

- All game code must include doc comments on public APIs
- Architecture decisions are recorded as ADRs in `docs/architecture/`. **How many is
  set by `modes.workflow`** — all ADRs at `full`, *critical* ADRs only at `standard`,
  and none required at `minimal`, where the decision log and `design/game-brief.md`
  carry the rationale instead. See `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.
- Gameplay values must be data-driven (external config), never hardcoded
- All public methods must be unit-testable (dependency injection over singletons)
- Commits must reference the relevant design document or task ID
- **Commit messages**: Use Conventional Commits format — `feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, `test:`, `refactor:`. Reference the story or task ID in the body (e.g., `Story: EPIC-001-S02`).
- **Verification-driven development**: Write tests first when adding gameplay systems.
  For UI changes, verify with screenshots. Compare expected output to actual output
  before marking work complete. Every implementation should have a way to prove it works.
- **A parse check is not a run.** Every story that changes something
  player-observable is launched and observed before it closes, and the
  observation is a retained screenshot in `production/qa/evidence/`. Procedure
  per engine: `.claude/docs/run-and-observe.md`. Not waived at
  `qa.level: minimal` — tests are, the look is not.

# Design Document Standards

- All design docs use Markdown
- Each mechanic has a dedicated document in `design/gdd/`
- **How many of the 8 sections are required depends on `modes.workflow`** —
  all 8 at `full`, 5 (+ Formulas when the system defines numeric rules — rates,
  curves, thresholds, costs; the system's `Category` is a hint, not the test) at
  `standard`, and no
  GDD at all at `minimal`, where `design/game-brief.md` is the design record.
  See `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`. The 8 sections:
  1. **Overview** -- one-paragraph summary
  2. **Player Fantasy** -- intended feeling and experience
  3. **Detailed Rules** -- unambiguous mechanics
  4. **Formulas** -- all math defined with variables
  5. **Edge Cases** -- unusual situations handled
  6. **Dependencies** -- other systems listed
  7. **Tuning Knobs** -- configurable values identified
  8. **Acceptance Criteria** -- testable success conditions
- Balance values must link to their source formula or rationale

# Testing Standards

## Test Evidence by Story Type

All stories must have appropriate test evidence before they can be marked Done:

| Story Type | Required Evidence | Location | Default Gate Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Logic** (formulas, AI, state machines) | Automated unit test — must pass | `tests/unit/[system]/` | BLOCKING |
| **Integration** (multi-system) | Integration test OR documented playtest | `tests/integration/[system]/` | BLOCKING |
| **Visual/Feel** (animation, VFX, feel) | Retained screenshot + lead sign-off | `production/qa/evidence/` | BLOCKING |
| **UI** (menus, HUD, screens) | Retained screenshot of each screen touched | `production/qa/evidence/` | BLOCKING |
| **Config/Data** (balance tuning) | Smoke check pass | `production/qa/smoke-[date].md` | ADVISORY |

The **Default Gate Level** applies when `testing.strict` is not set in
`project.yaml`. A project may override it per test type: `testing.strict.logic`,
`.integration`, `.visual`, `.ui`, and `.config` each take `true` (BLOCKING) or
`false` (ADVISORY). `/story-done`, `/story-readiness`, `/dev-story`,
`/gate-check`, and `/smoke-check` resolve the effective level from that setting,
falling back to the defaults above when it is absent.

> **Why Visual and UI block.** "Retained" is load-bearing — the screenshot must
> still be on disk in `production/qa/evidence/` when the story is closed. One
> that was captured and discarded is an assertion, not evidence. These two rows
> block because for a game the way it looks *is* the product: an advisory visual
> gate gets deferred in favour of whatever does block, and the result is a
> well-tested game that looks wrong.

> **Exception — `/smoke-check`.** The ADVISORY default for **Config/Data** above
> applies to *per-story evidence* gates. `/smoke-check` is a build-health gate,
> not a per-story evidence gate, so its own unset default for
> `testing.strict.config` is **BLOCKING**. The two defaults differ on purpose.

## Automated Test Rules

- **Naming**: per engine — `.claude/rules/test-standards.md`
- **Determinism**: Tests must produce the same result every run — no random seeds, no time-dependent assertions
- **Isolation**: Each test sets up and tears down its own state; tests must not depend on execution order
- **No hardcoded data**: Test fixtures use constant files or factory functions, not inline magic numbers
  (exception: boundary value tests where the exact number IS the point)
- **Independence**: Unit tests do not call external APIs, databases, or file I/O — use dependency injection

## What NOT to Automate

- Visual fidelity (shader output, VFX appearance, animation curves)
- "Feel" qualities (input responsiveness, perceived weight, timing)
- Platform-specific rendering (test on target hardware, not headlessly)
- Full gameplay sessions (covered by playtesting, not automation)

## CI/CD Rules

- Automated test suite runs on every push to main and every PR
- No merge if tests fail — tests are a blocking gate in CI
- Never disable or skip failing tests to make CI pass — fix the underlying issue
- Engine-specific CI commands:
  - **Godot**: `godot --headless -s -d --remote-debug tcp://127.0.0.1:0 res://addons/gdUnit4/bin/GdUnitCmdTool.gd -a res://tests --ignoreHeadlessMode`
  - **Unity**: `game-ci/unity-test-runner@v4` (GitHub Actions)
  - **Unreal**: headless runner with `-nullrhi` flag

# Advisor Tool

You have access to an `advisor` tool backed by a stronger reviewer model. It takes NO parameters -- when you call advisor(), your entire conversation history is automatically forwarded. They see the task, every tool call you've made, every result you've seen.

Call advisor BEFORE substantive work -- before writing, before committing to an interpretation, before building on an assumption. If the task requires orientation first (finding files, fetching a source, seeing what's there), do that, then call advisor. Orientation is not substantive work. Writing, editing, and declaring an answer are.

Also call advisor:
- When you believe the task is complete. BEFORE this call, make your deliverable durable: write the file, save the result, commit the change. The advisor call takes time; if the session ends during it, a durable result persists and an unwritten one doesn't.
- When stuck -- errors recurring, approach not converging, results that don't fit.
- When considering a change of approach.

On tasks longer than a few steps, call advisor at least once before committing to an approach and once before declaring done. On short reactive tasks where the next action is dictated by tool output you just read, you don't need to keep calling -- the advisor adds most of its value on the first call, before the approach crystallizes.

Give the advice serious weight. If you follow a step and it fails empirically, or you have primary-source evidence that contradicts a specific claim (the file says X, the paper states Y), adapt. A passing self-test is not evidence the advice is wrong -- it's evidence your test doesn't check what the advice is checking.

If you've already retrieved data pointing one way and the advisor points another: don't silently switch. Surface the conflict in one more advisor call -- "I found X, you suggest Y, which constraint breaks the tie?" The advisor saw your evidence but may have underweighted it; a reconcile call is cheaper than committing to the wrong branch.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
